name: Jade Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the postnatal ward at a small district hospital, so mums and babies after the birth. My shift is checking stitches and blood loss, helping with feeding, newborn checks, and a lot of teaching first-time parents how to bath a baby without panicking. I love the mornings when a family goes home happy. What wears me out is the night shifts and when we're one midwife and two nurses short on a full ward.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Luke two years ago. He's an electrician, works for himself mostly, rewiring old houses. We rent a semi on the edge of town near my parents and we've got about four months saved. We'd like a baby next year, if things go well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That wouldn't surprise me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people get carried away with new gadgets. I'd say it to my friends at church and my mum, not online, I don't really post opinions. Hard work and family are what actually keep you going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, nothing really changes for me. Babies don't care about AI, they still arrive at three in the morning and still need someone to help them latch. Luke's still got more work than he can handle. So I'd feel fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. Finish my postnatal competencies, keep saving for when the baby comes, and maybe use AI now and then for meal planning or writing my reflective notes. Look at midwifery training in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, really. I'd be thinking about baby names, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would having a baby mean for your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go part-time for a few years. Luke earns enough that we'd manage with that, and my mum lives ten minutes away. That's how we've planned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything bothering you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's high, and being junior means I still get the worst shifts. But that's normal. It'll get better.

say: People get **carried away** with new gadgets every few years.
**Hard work and family** are what really keep you going.
think: Nothing really changes for me, because **babies** still need help.
Luke still has **more work** than he can handle.
do: Look at **midwifery training** in a few years.
feel: **Calm** and settled, thinking about baby names.
S0.quote: Babies don't care about AI, they still arrive at three in the morning and still need someone to help them latch.
fieldNote: Two **hands-on incomes** and nearby family make her secure.
She'd go **part-time** after a baby, as planned.
Her outlook is rooted in **church and family**.

steps.text: Finish her postnatal competencies on the maternity ward
Save toward going part-time after the baby
Plan to start a family with Luke next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and planning. So the paperwork gets easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it could help nurses if it frees up time for patients. If a computer writes my discharge notes, I get ten more minutes with a new mum who's crying because feeding isn't working. I'd say that in the staff room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's mostly good for me. My job's hands-on and Luke's is too. The office people at the hospital would have it harder, and I'd feel for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools once the others had tried them and said they worked. I'd keep saving, keep to the baby plan. I might look at the midwifery course sooner if the ward changed a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of curiosity about what changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust AI with anything about a newborn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the paperwork, yes. With the baby, no. A computer can't feel if a baby is floppy or hot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ward clerk, Pam, and the booking staff. They're lovely and they're the ones on your card.

say: AI could help if it **frees up time** for patients.
I'd say that in the **staff room**, not online.
think: It's **mostly good** for me, since both our jobs are hands-on.
The **office people** at the hospital would have it harder.
do: Use AI tools once **colleagues** say they work.
Keep **saving** and keep the baby plan.
Look at **midwifery** sooner if the ward changes a lot.
feel: **Calm**, with some curiosity about what changes.
S1.quote: If a computer writes my discharge notes, I get ten more minutes with a new mum who's crying because feeding isn't working.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a **paperwork** helper, never a baby carer.
Both household jobs are **hands-on**, which keeps her calm.
She'd adopt tools **after colleagues** prove them.

steps.text: Use AI discharge notes once colleagues confirm they work
Keep saving about £150 a month toward the baby
Stick to the plan of a first baby next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then robots by 2031. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will need to stick together, because I don't trust the government to sort it. I'd say businesses should keep people in work where they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me. My husband wires houses and I look after new mums, and by 2031 a robot might be doing both of those jobs. We'd have a baby by then, maybe two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the baby off a year and save hard, aiming for eight months of savings. I'd look at midwifery training straight away, because births feel like the last thing a robot would do. Luke would get into solar and battery installs, which are booming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but worried about timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're a team and we'll work it out. He'd say electricians will always be needed. I'd want to believe him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would delaying the baby be hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. My mum would be upset too. But I'd rather wait a year than struggle with a newborn and no income.

say: Families and **communities** will need to stick together.
**Businesses** should keep people in work where they can, not just cut.
think: Both our **hands-on jobs** could go by 2031.
We'd have a **baby** by then, maybe two, depending on those jobs.
do: Delay the **baby** by a year and save hard.
Help Luke move into **solar and battery** installs.
S2.quote: My husband wires houses and I look after new mums, and by 2031 a robot might be doing both of those jobs.
fieldNote: Both jobs are hands-on, so the **2031 robots** hit them together.
She'd **delay the baby**, which is painful for her.
Her trust sits with **family and business**, not government.

steps.text: Delay the first baby by a year
Save hard toward eight months of costs
Apply for a midwifery training place straight away
Help Luke buy kit for solar and battery installs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same: families stick together, businesses keep people working. And people should take responsibility to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years means we can still have our first baby in 2027 and I can train as a midwife before the robots get anywhere near a labour ward. Luke would have time to build his solar work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Baby in 2027, as planned. Midwifery training starting around 2029, part-time. Keep saving. Use AI tools as they become normal on the ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. There's time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you manage training with a toddler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum. She's already offered to have the baby two days a week. That's what family's for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the robots come earlier than they say. Five years can become three.

say: Families should stick together and **businesses** keep people working.
People should **take responsibility** to prepare, not wait for someone else.
think: We can still have our **first baby** in 2027.
I can train as a **midwife** before robots reach labour wards.
do: Use **AI tools** as they become normal.
feel: **Uneasy**, but okay, with time to plan.
S3.quote: Five years means we can still have our first baby in 2027 and I can train as a midwife before the robots get anywhere near a labour ward.
fieldNote: Five years lets her keep the **baby plan** intact.
She fears the five-year timeline could **shrink** to three unexpectedly.

steps.text: Have the first baby in 2027 as planned
Use the ward's AI tools as they become normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels like plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so families and communities can prepare properly. No need for panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, with ten years, we can have our family first and worry about the robots when our kids are at school. I'd be a midwife by then, hopefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Baby next year, maybe another in 2029. Midwifery training when the kids are small. Keep saving. Luke builds up his business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years feels like a lifetime when you're planning a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your kids to go into nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to do something that helps people and uses their hands. Whatever that is by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the ten years go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we just sat back. We won't.

say: We've got time, so **families and communities** can prepare.
There's **no need for panic** with ten years to get ready.
think: We can have our **family first** and worry about robots later.
I'd hopefully be a **midwife** before the robots come.
do: Have a **baby** next year and maybe another in 2029.
Train in **midwifery** when the kids are small.
feel: **Calm**, because ten years feels like a lifetime.
S4.quote: With ten years, we can have our family first and worry about the robots when our kids are at school.
fieldNote: With a decade, her **family plans** stay untouched.
She trusts her **own effort** to make the time count.
Luke's **business** is part of the household plan.

steps.text: Have a first baby next year and maybe another in 2029
Train as a midwife while the children are small
Help Luke grow his electrical business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both Luke and I would be hit within a few years, just when we'd want to start a family. What would help is warning, honestly, and training places for midwives so people like me can move into it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people would do for themselves. Nobody's going to hand my family a living, so I want enough warning to sort it out myself.

headlineQuote: Nobody's going to hand my family a living, so I want enough warning to sort it out myself.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old junior nurse** on a postnatal ward, married to Luke, an electrician.
They rent near her parents with about **four months saved** and plan a baby next year.
She's **traditional**, trusting family and business more than government.
She stays **calm** in slow pictures but becomes anxious when robots threaten both hands-on jobs by 2031.
Her plan in every picture is **midwifery training** and keeping her family plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both incomes could go just as they start a family.
